beats.intro: Lesson seven. [[sub]]How to run your own week like a well-planned factory.
beats.speed: The third way to raise your output is to work faster. [[eq]]Output per hour is leverage times activities per hour. [[tips]]Time-management advice attacks the hours: handle each paper once, hold stand-up meetings, turn your desk away from the door. [[better]]Grove does better by borrowing from production.
beats.limit: First, find your limiting step. [[fix]]Some things are truly fixed. For Grove, it was a class with over two hundred students waiting. [[prep]]Preparation has to happen before it, offset like toast before the egg. [[rest]]Everything that can move is scheduled around what cannot.
beats.batch: Second, batch similar work. [[setup]]Every task needs some set-up time, the way switching the egg boiler to four-minute eggs means adjusting and testing. [[one]]Do six reviews on six different days, and you pay that set-up six times. [[group]]Do them in one block, and you pay it once. [[reuse]]The same goes for reusing the slides you made for one class in the next.
beats.calendar: Third, a factory runs on a forecast. A job shop takes whatever walks in. [[much]]Much of a manager's work can be forecast. [[shop]]Yet most of us use the calendar as a list of orders: someone asks for time, and it simply appears. Grove calls that mindless passivity. [[plan]]Use it as a production plan instead. [[fill]]Set the fixed events, then fill the gaps yourself with work that is necessary but not time-critical.
beats.no: A factory will not start material it cannot finish. [[jam]]Start too much, and work stalls halfway, behind a bottleneck, where it is worth more. [[gate]]So say no at the outset, to work beyond your capacity. [[late]]A late no wastes more, and not delivering is a no anyway. [[yes]]Remember, every yes to one thing is a no to something else.
beats.slack: Next, allow slack. [[road]]A freeway carries the most cars at one ideal level of traffic. [[jam]]Add just a few more, and everything grinds to a halt. That is why on-ramps are metered. [[day]]Load your day the same way: full, but with enough slack [[call]]that one unexpected call does not wreck the rest of it.
beats.inventory: At the same time, keep an inventory, of projects. [[wip]]Not work in process, which spoils like eggs left in the boiler. [[raw]]Raw material: things that need doing but not finishing today, that improve your team over the long term. [[idle]]Without that stock, free time tends to turn into meddling. [[std]]And when a method works, reuse it, but keep thinking about why it works.
beats.q3: Quick check. Name the production idea.
beats.span: How many people should report to you? [[few]]Too few, and your leverage drops. [[many]]Too many, and you get bogged down. [[rule]]Grove's rule of thumb: six to eight, for a manager whose work is mostly supervising. [[half]]It comes from about half a day a week for each person. [[two]]Two days a week each would lead to meddling. [[hour]]One hour is not enough to monitor. [[know]]Know-how managers count differently. Half a day a week on a planning or advisory group counts as one report.
beats.plant: Sometimes the structure fights the rule. [[two]]A plant manager has only two reports: engineering and manufacturing. [[risk]]With so few, he risks retiring on the job, or meddling. [[act]]So he acts as his own engineering manager. [[six]]Now he has six direct reports: five engineers, plus the manufacturing manager. [[level]]Draw it so the engineers do not appear at the same level as the manufacturing manager. He would rightly object.
beats.regular: Production loves regularity. [[arr]]The breakfast factory would run better if customers came in a steady stream, not in ones and twos. [[smooth]]You cannot control everyone, but you can smooth your own load, [[bomb]]and look into the black box for time bombs, so you deal with them when you choose, not when they go off. [[mon]]Regularity also needs others to join in. At Intel, Monday mornings were set aside for planning groups, everywhere.
beats.interrupt: About twenty managers once paired up, one as client, one as consultant, to find what most limited their output. [[top]]The most common answer: uncontrolled interruptions. [[who]]They came from reports, and from the people who use the manager's authority and information. [[hide]]The favourite fixes were to hide, or to ask customers not to call at certain hours. [[no]]But interrupters have real problems. Hide, and the problems simply pile up.
beats.fixes: Grove borrows from production instead. [[std]]Most interruptions repeat, so prepare standard answers, which others can also give. [[batch]]Batch the questions from your reports into one-on-ones and staff meetings. [[arch]]Keep indicators on file, so answers take seconds. [[sign]]And ask people to decide whether it can wait: a sign that says, unless it really cannot wait until two o'clock, [[hour]]plus an office hour where you are fully available. [[reg]]The principle: make the irregular regular.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[w1]]Plan around the fixed points, and batch similar work. [[w2]]Use your calendar as a production plan, and say no early. [[w3]]Leave slack, and keep a stock of projects. [[w4]]Six to eight reports, at about half a day a week each. [[w5]]Channel interruptions into regular times and standard answers. Now the lesson practice.

beats.finish: Well done. That is the end of lesson seven.
